Consequently, developing robust mechanisms to harness this vast information has become paramount, particularly through rigorous statistical incident detection methods for anomaly identification. This endeavor is often complicated by contextual variability, which necessitates approaches capable of managing mechanisms, environments, and operating conditions in their dynamic states. To address this, we present **g-DID**, a novel detection framework designed for dynamic graphs. By integrating standard deviation calculations with degree-based analysis, the g-DID model effectively accounts for both time and spatial dimensions. Empirically, our results demonstrate that the graph-based detection algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art methodologies.

This research investigates the adiabatic shock jump across a planar interface within an ideal gas that separates two media of distinct densities, focusing on the dynamic expansion of a shock that penetrates the interface. As time progresses indefinitely, the motion stabilizes into a steady state characterized by a shock moving at a constant velocity. The study analyzes how the magnitude of this ultimate velocity depends on the initial conditions of the moving boundary and the properties of the adjacent ideal fluids. Furthermore, the work presents the evolution of this velocity over time and examines how the initial shock jump geometry and the densities of both surrounding media influence this front. Special attention is given to the scenario where the shock moves from a denser to a less dense environment, detailing how resolution mechanisms function as they approach the steady regime. While earlier research addressed this phenomenon in a uniform homogeneous background, that context often yields an infinitely continuous set of possible steady velocities when dealing a mismatched second medium. In contrast, this study provides a clear, unique determination of that limiting velocity for any given boundary movement profile, specifically identifying how a accelerating start settles into a constant transit rate.

Engineering systems that interact with users through complex and often puzzling AI-driven functionalities, such as opaque decision-making or excessive data processing, presents significant challenges, particularly regarding usability. Since prior research confirms that human cognition is heavily constrained by limited memory and engagement during tasks, poor system interfaces can detrimentally affect performance. In this paper, we advocate for an approach grounded in cognitive constraints to enhance system interfaces by understanding how users perceive functional capabilities, particularly under conditions of obscurity. Specifically, we introduce a systematic technique to gather clarity-oriented needs through interviews, with the ultimate goal of addressing functional requirements in more cognitively aligned ways. We validate this methodology by applying it to the domain of explainability, where we demonstrate its efficacy using a real-world case study from the automotive industry.

The identification and characterization of colorectal polyps during endoscopic examinations serve as an essential step in preventing colorectal cancer (CRC). Within the context of the 2020 Screen & Treat Endoscopic Subtask of the Pathological Image Grand Challenge on Colorectal Cancer, this work analyzes histopathological images of colorectal tissues. We introduce **UniToPatho**, a dataset comprising 1,100 annotated tissue sections that depict examples of both normal and malignant tumors alongside grading information for adenomas. Utilizing the rich annotation data within our colony, we have developed **UniUniNormalizer**, which refines the visual features of histological images to enhance model performance. Furthermore, we present **PathoSegmenter**, an advanced methodology for segmenting these tissues. Extensive experimental results validate our findings, placing our contributions in second overall rank within the competitive challenge.

Recently, our authors introduced an innovative framework for source encoding that surpasses traditional Markov assumptions to model dependencies among neighboring samples. Depending on neighboring context during the generation of every single sample, this method constructs a locally varied partition of the source domain. Depending on their distribution within this partition, local decoders produce final outputs that offer superior recovery accuracy when neighboring data is more precisely regained with higher fidelity. Although effective at enhancing image restoration performance with superior visual quality, this approach risks exposing sensitive information during the training phase of downstream machine learning systems due closely correlated neighboring data. Consequently, this work proposes investigating data leakage risks in Markov source coding, specifically examining how such correlations compromise privacy in machine learning applications alongside evaluating the information-theoretic bounds of leakage. Our findings indicate that although these source-coded data sets often outperform standard benchmarks regarding accuracy metrics, they remain vulnerable to substantial security risks involving intricate source distributions that result in significant performance degradation in downstream modeling tasks, ultimately suggesting possible improvements through enhanced bound refinements or architectural adjustments in machine learning systems themselves as a means of achieving greater security standards.

Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images are frequently degraded by impulsive noise, which significantly impedes the accuracy of subsequent radar analyses. Although denoising autoencoders (DNAs) have become a popular machine learning approach for addressing these issues, they suffer from two primary limitations: the inability to distinguish between noisy and clean data during training, and their tendency to function as local optimizers trapped in suboptimal results. To address these challenges, we have developed the Deep Prior Denosing Self-Contained model for Synthetic Aperture Radar, known as MrSARP. This architecture serves as a generative hierarchical prior that explicitly categorizes inputs based on the presence of noise. Furthermore, MrSARP performs as an autonomous model that does not rely on paired training datasets, thereby addressing the data scarcity often encountered in SAR applications. We evaluated the architecture against various state-of-the-art techniques using both real and simulated SAR datasets. The impulse noise removal capability of MrSARP has been verified through quantitative and qualitative metrics, demonstrating its competitive performance relative to existing solutions.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) represents an approach using variational quantum circuits for solving combinatorial optimization issues. Despite its potential as variation for solving these problems, so far AQA has struggled in terms with Q for addressing optimization issues. Here we introduce an enhanced QAOA with better performance achieved by using Bayesian methods to enhance its results. By applying this new algorithm, we outperform other current methods. Using well-known graph types to test our new approach, such as Max-Cut and Maximum Satisfiability problems, demonstrates how effective this approach is compared to current methods.

We have developed an approach to calculate the overlapping area between two ellipses, regardless of their relative positions, orientation, or size. This computation breaks the complex area into a set of characteristic regions: potentially zero, one, or two ellipsing profiles and zero to two triangles. Utilizing region-specific formulas, we determine each segment's area. For circular cases, we calculate intersection areas via a simple, closed-form equation. However, the determination of each ellipse's profile area relies on an efficient algorithm that evaluates intersection points between an arbitrary circle and a target ellipse, followed by the numerical quadrature application (specifically Gaussian quadrature) to find the area under any positive function. We conclude the discussion by suggesting a method to compute the area of two ellipsing profiles as a limit process involving circle-ellipse intersections, effectively allowing the calculation of overlaps between any pair of non-circular ellipsing shapes.

Online reinforcement learning (RL) has proven to be a powerful method for discovering optimal policies across numerous domains, including robotics and gaming. While the field of multi-armed bandits serves as the foundational starting point for online RL, the core decision-making process involves selecting an untried arm with a high expected reward versus pulling a known arm to gather more information. This inherent trade-off is often modeled as the exploration-exploitation dilemma. Originally, this concept was formalized within the stochastic setting of multi-armed bandits by Ucsa and van Rijn (1990), later extending to continuous durations proposed by Dean et al. (2018). However, both environments assume environmental transitions are stochastic with deterministic structures, failing to reflect complex, high-dimensional, and nonlinear realities found in fields like robotics. Consequently, there is a pressing need to advance the theoretical framework of extended multi-armed bandids to encompass non-stochastic, nonlinear dynamics. This paper proposes a novel algorithm and accompanying theoretical guarantees for exploring continuous-duration environments under nonlinear conditions. The authors present a theoretical analysis demonstrating the performance of their proposed 'q-Learning-style' framework. Furthermore, extensive evaluations on various synthetic benchmarks and real-world robotics tasks confirm the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

We investigate the low-energy magnetic fluctuations in half-filled electrons on system A using exact quantum impurity techniques within the two-leg ladder structure. Results derived implicity from exact solutions indicate persistent short-range antiferromagnetic (AFM) correlations regardless of filling level, concurrently suppressing any potential development in both charge spin in both neutral d and dopant scenarios. Nevertheless, considerable doping levels trigger a transition into a spin-doped Mott state characterized by emergent long-range helical magnetism at low energy. Our findings regarding the suppression of magnetic order are interpreted as stemming from enhanced phase space for spin-3/2 excitations inherent to the system's structure, which energetically favor single-particle (SDW) states over alternative descriptions. Additionally, we analyze how specific patterns of magnetic doping induce specific descriptions, leading us to formulate specific descriptions, leading us to refine existing theoretical models to encompass these impurities. Additionally, we analyze how specific patterns of magnetic doping induce specific descriptions, leading us to refine existing theoretical models to encompass these impurities. Specifically, we refine the standard phase diagram to account for these specific conditions.

Precise localization and indexing of vertebrae are crucial for assessing spinal deformities like idiopathic scoliosis within medical imaging. However, prevalent methods depend heavily or entirely on manual input, which limits their widespread adoption in clinical settings due to restricted availability. While numerous automatic algorithms exist, many lack sufficient accuracy to facilitate effective patient care. This paper introduces fully autonomous methodologies to localize and index vertebrae in computed tomography (CT) images, built upon a workflow that rectifies the spine and aligns it with a canonical orientation, followed by fine-tuning vertebrae positions using anatomical constraints. Experiments validated these methodologies across two datasets, covering both clinical CT cases and CT-derived synthetic 3D MRI sets, revealing that approximately 90% of vertebrae achieved classification accuracy, precision, and recall of at least 0.90. Visualization comparisons against existing techniques underscored these superior statistical outcomes.

Stochastic Thermodynamics models physical systems by representing their evolution through random jump processes defined at the mesoscale. In this framework, system currents emerge as emergent properties generated by superimposing numerous discrete sample paths, with their amplitudes diminishing relative to the total number of possible paths as system resolution increases to a continuum limit. Using a formalism capable of generating current fluctuation distributions directly—bypassing the need to first construct the underlying trajectory dynamics—we demonstrate that in the asymptotic limit, these current fluctuations conform to a chiral symmetric spectrum paired with corresponding cumulants for intensities. Furthermore, we show how chiral symmetry inherently enforces linear relations among certain higher-order fluctuation terms. These observations serve as initial validations for Stochastic Thermodynamics as a distinct framework designed specifically for trajectory-level fluctuations.

In this paper, we explore the Hamiltonian framework of relative quantum geometry for Kähler manifolds that are Hilbert polynomial- equivalent and share k-dimensional positive part structures, specifically utilizing a relative Fubini-Sture metric within a common functional class of relative Kähler potentials. The dynamics governing relative quantum geometry are defined relative to the Hamiltonian of a chosen relative Hamiltonian function through its relative Fubini-Sture metric. Our study focuses on the derivation of key geometric quantities—including the relative Fubini-Sture metric, relative holomorphic and anti-holomorphic two-forms, relative Christoff  symbols, relative Ricci curvature, and the associated Riemann manifold structure—examining how these elements transform via their respective Hamiltonian evolution laws. These transformation rules are validated and illustrated by applying them to reblowing processes on algebraic varieties that demonstrate Kähler manifold equivalence based on their Hilbert polynomial restrictions.

Piezoacoustic resonators are widely utilized within the time-to-digital-converter (TTC) systems of hadron and lepton colliders to measure time with great precision. These colliders demand a high degree of isolation, meaning that electrical connections to a resonator should ideally generate mechanical strains undetectable at neighboring resonators. Departures from this ideal isolation have previously been observed when Au ground supports holding Ge piezoacoustic crystals are subjected to epimetal changes during annealing. In this study, we achieve near-perfect mechanical coupling, reaching 98% transmission of piezoacoustic waves, by using an Al Aluminium Al alloy instead of Au for the Ge resonator's mount. Furthermore, we have evaluated the mechanical properties and identified the constituent microstructural elements of this novel Al alloy microstructure through microstructure characterization.

Nonlinear optics within reservoir engineering enables diverse applications, ranging from single-shot imaging and computing to agnostic machine learning. While traditional approaches rely on ensemble statistical analyses, it is proven that at higher densities, two excitations can interact via nonlinear effects within these reservoirs. This interaction arises specifically from exciton-polariton systems, which are capable of global condensates. Consequently, the unique nonlinearity found in these systems allows for the operation of large-scale computing devices based on nonlinear optics using fully coherent reservoir ensembles, thereby extending the domain of reservoir optics.

The recent identification of dust sublimation rings close to the habit zones of stars suggests a continuous escape of planetary material in the form of rings consisting of vaporized particles. By utilizing the Gran Telescopio Canarias with a new technique based on the Maxwell equations within near-infrared linear polarization measurements, we have determined that the polarization phase curve of K2-22 b exhibits a best-fit model requiring a monodisperse ring of optically thick dust at a 1.0 AU semi-major axis. This model consists of non-volatile spherical particles with a radius of 10 micrometers that reach equilibrium temperatures of 600 Kelvin. Our findings indicate these particles exist in a pressure-supported, optically thick environment with a vertical thickness 1.5 times their own diameter. These particles likely coexist with volatile components volatile at equivalent temperatures. We have detected a mass loss rate of $1.5 \times 10^{11}$ kg/year of dust alone, implying an upper limit on the total planetary mass loss of $2.2 \times 10^{11}$ kg/year. This observation highlights that the companion to K2-22 is undergoing hydrodynamic escape, and we provide a method to place tighter constraints on the volatile fraction of such exoplanets.

We offer fresh proofs demonstrating the coherence of the Milnor fiber across complex spaces with isolated singularities. Previously established by Garn in 2006 for smooth varieties, this property critically influences various aspects of complex analytic geometry; our contributions build upon techniques from their work by extending them to the broader context of isolated singularities. Furthermore, leveraging recent findings by Hartshorne (2021), we demonstrate a landscape-independent coherence for the Milnor fiber surrounding rational singularities—a scenario where traditional methods encounter fundamental limitations. To establish coherence locally near each singular fiber, we first prove a foundational result characterizing the rational singularity: such a singularity occurs precisely when the associated Milnor fiber exhibits reduced singularities on a normal surface. This characterization holds particular significance through a linear map connecting two morphisms to show equivalence between rationality in singularities and the normality and reduced conditions of specific associated fibers.

In 2022, approximately 20% of all websites relied on Google Analytics for data reporting. This paper introduces Daany, a flexible framework designed to extract information from web trajectories. As demonstrated by our evaluation on 140 popular websites using public browser inspection tools, public JavaScript present on these sites supports trajectory extraction via 46 distinct API integrations. We believe Daany will benefit researchers, such as cognitive scientists, whose current access to analytic software is restricted by financial constraints.

This paper investigates how Galileo conceptualized thinking versus calculating, highlighting his famous claim from *Discourses* that the mind's role is similar to just providing inputs for nature to actively work on. Despite being a pioneering physicist famous for his thinking achievements, Galileo illustrated his point using mathematical operations to connect cognitive processes with numerical activity. However, modern scholars struggle to interpret why he made this specific connection between mental activity and math.

Recombination occurs when the early universe cools to a threshold where hydrogen atoms form, causing a decoupling of radiation from matter. Because hydrogen formation releases photons that cannot escape, these recombination events create a chromospheric layer extending roughly ten e-folding times beyond the radiation horizon, distorting both the radiation spectrum and the expansion dynamics. While standard cosmological models treat this epoch as having 4 e-folding thickness based on prior simulations, our findings using full time-dependent simulations reveal significant impacts on cosmic history when modeling it instead with 10 e-folding thickness. Specifically, we observe shifts in the Hubble constant and CMB power spectrum behavior during recombination due to increased non-linear gravitational effects and local energy transport. Furthermore, modeling with double the estimated thickness yields lower mu-mode power at specific scales alongside enhanced sensitivity to recombination physics parameters and greater allowed deviations of primordial helium abundance from Saha equilibrium predictions. Consequently, incorporating these extended structural effects regarding the hydrogen epoch proves vital for refining constraints on early universe evolution within high-precision cosmological frameworks.

In collisional plasmas, magnetic reconnection is typically constrained by the slow electron diffusion process. Nevertheless, when these plasmas exhibit low levels of collisionality, localized regions can form where the effective electron cyclotronic frequency surpasses both the magnetic and iterative recombination rates, restoring fast, noncollational recombination mechanisms. These transiently achieved conditions allow researchers to isolate where noncollational effects dominate by integrating a hybrid approach: adapting the magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) framework with locally embedded particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations. In a series of magnetohydrodynamics hybrid models, we compare the dynamics of magnetic island coalescence across varying ratios of parallel collision frequencies to electron cyclotronic frequencies. By embedding PIC calculations within selected islands during the merger event, we observe modifications in both temporal and spatial profiles of the recombination rate as ratio changes the plasma environment.

This study introduces Ammanusens—a novel dynamic framework designed to automatically generate documentation and source code snippets directly from implementation code. Unlike current approaches that rely on pre-written examples or implementation logs to produce code snippets, the framework leverages a neutrals-style technique grounded in type inference. By analyzing the architectural structure and module interactions identified during the software development lifecycle, the system generates corresponding source segments and explains their functional purpose through the use of "types." Manifest types represent what a specific function achieves through the use of type names, while kind type represent functional capabilities through the use of type names. These two complementary type together constitute the neutrals-style technique used in this research. By employing these kind of type names, each function's functionality can ultimately be expressed in both concise type names and implementable type names. Key contributions include defining the Amanusens neutrals-style technique and demonstrating its application via a real-world research into how a database management system handles transaction processing. Through an in-depth examination of how type names and type names interact, the research reveals fresh perspectives on documenting complex algorithms and functions that are often difficult to understand even for experienced developers. Types Names: Type inference, type checking, type transformation, type synthesis, type documentation, type code generation.
